News.title: Siblings face £250k bill after neighbours' 'systematic destruction' tree claim
News.content:
Siblings face £250k bill after neighbours' 'systematic destruction' tree claim

Robert and Amanda McCarthy are seeking £250,000 in court over what they have claimed was the 'systematic destruction' of Leylandii trees at their home in Nazeing, Essex

View 4 Images Robert McCarthy and his wife claimed their neighbours destroyed their property by tearing down the leylandii trees (Image: Champion News)

Siblings could could be left with a "ruinous" quarter-of-a-million-pound court bill after invading their neighbours' "immaculate" garden and hacking down their 33-foot Leylandii trees.

Robert McCarthy and his wife Amanda lived for years in "relative harmony" alongside their neighbour, Foulla Bowler, and the two siblings she owns her house with. But a row over the boundary between their gardens broke out in 2018, and the couple sued over a row of 33-foot-tall Leylandii trees which were removed over "overshadowing" complaints.

Mrs Bowler, her brother John Barberis and sister Mary Englishby pulled out their back fence and had tree surgeons remove the trees, which the suing couple claimed in court amounted to "systematic destruction".

Lawyer explains what to do if neighbours break new March 31 bin rules READ MORE :

View 4 Images A court found the neighbours had trespassed on the couple's property to cut the trees down (Image: Getty Images)

The couple told Central London County Court the "systematic destruction" of their garden in the village of Nazeing, Essex, had completely ruined the privacy of their home, demanding almost £250,000 in costs and damages. Following a trial, Judge Alan Saggerson has now ruled in favour of the couple on the location of the boundary, finding that the siblings had "trespassed" into their neighbours' garden to hack down the trees.

The trio had taken "unilateral action to re-order the disputed boundary" between the properties amid what he called "fence wars" between the neighbours.

The full cost of the case to the siblings will be decided later, but the decision means they are likely to be liable for the McCarthys' lawyers' bills, which are estimated at £130,000, on top of their own significant court costs - plus potentially as much as £115,000 in compensation.

"This is a protracted and potentially ruinous boundary dispute between neighbours," said the judge in his judgment, which was only made public last week.

During the trial last October, the judge was told that civil construction manager Mr McCarthy, 59, and his carer wife, Amanda, 61, bought their home in Common View, Bumbles Green, Nazeing, in 2001. The house, which Mrs McCarthy said had an "immaculate, very pleasant garden" when they moved in, is bordered to the rear by the home of Mrs Bowler, 61, known as Kormakitis.

It had been Mrs Bowler's family home as a teenager, but she now lives there with her own family and it is owned by her, along with her two siblings, John Barberis, 63, and Mary Englishby, 59.

Barrister Christopher Coyle, for the McCarthys, told the judge that the two gardens were divided by a fence, with a row of Leylandii trees on the McCarthys' side. However, a bitter boundary dispute erupted around 2018, with Mrs Bowler and her siblings claiming the dividing line was actually beyond the fence, putting the Leylandii on their land.

View 4 Images The decision means the siblings are likely to be liable for the McCarthys' lawyers' bills (Image: Champion News)

And, despite knowing that there was a dispute, Mrs Bowler had in 2018 applied for permission to fell 29 trees, before the family went ahead with the plan, cutting down most of them in January 2022.

Mr Coyle said the felling work had continued into a second day even though the McCarthys wrote to the siblings via lawyers to request them to stop cutting. Giving evidence, Mr McCarthy described it as an "invasion" and complained of a "relentless destruction of my garden," telling the judge: "This is how we feel as a family."

"I can stand upstairs in my house and they can see me walking around," he said from the witness box. "I want my privacy back like I had."

He said that, when the couple bought the house, they were led to believe that the fence beyond the trees was the boundary, making the trees part of their property. The trees were well-established when we moved in," he told the judge. "We thought the chain link fence was the boundary as it ran along. I had no reason not to believe that to be the boundary."

The McCarthys sued for about £115,000 in compensation, including £73,500 to plant new trees and restore their privacy, as well as a declaration that the true boundary is the line of the old fence.

But Mrs Bowler and her siblings insisted that they had every right to remove the fence and trees as they were in fact on their land, and that they removed them due to "overshadowing" and potential damage to their land. Her brother, Mr Barberis, said he was there in 1981 when their father, Elias Barberis, discussed buying Kormakitis and remembers hearing that the boundary was several feet beyond the fence. It was his father who had planted the trees.

"Some of the trees are missing, not all of them," he added, when pressed on their felling. "These are trees that we planted and a fence that we put up."

"I clearly remember our parents giving [the previous owner] permission to trim our trees from his side to stop them overshadowing his garden." Giving judgment, Judge Saggerson said the siblings' evidence was "less reliable and less accurate" than the McCarthys', but did not find they were lying, but instead had "persuaded themselves of the righteousness of their own case."

He said the chain link fence had been there in 1981 and was probably there at the latest in 1975, with wooden panels later put in place along it.

‌



However, he said he did not accept that the siblings' father had been told when buying Kormakitis in 1981 that his land extended 6ft beyond the line of the fence. "I do not accept that he had any reasonable grounds for believing this, although over the passage of many years he may have persuaded himself that this was the position," he said.

View 4 Images Mrs Bowler and the siblings claimed the Leylandii were on their land (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

"Unfortunately, as I find, the defendants took unilateral action to re-order the disputed boundary." Their father, with his son John present, had begun by starting to take the fence down in May 2018, with plants then being pulled up in the face of objections from Mr McCarthy.

‌



Despite a replacement fence being put up by Mr McCarthy, the siblings again removed it in May the following year, before removing another in February 2020.

"On 3 March 2020, a tree surgeon instructed by the defendants attended and started removing trees from their garden and also started taking out other planting along the disputed boundary," said the judge. "In early January 2022, the tree surgeons returned. They cut down the remaining trees along the disputed boundary, completely removing the privacy screen that had existed for so many years.

"Due to the defendants' unilateral action, the landscape along the disputed boundary has completely changed from that which existed before May 2018."

Article continues below

Having heard expert evidence, he said the original fence line was the "true boundary," placing the Leylandii trees in the McCarthys' garden. That tallied with the historic attitude and behaviour of the two sets of neighbours in respect of the boundary, he said, finding that all of them, plus Elias Barberis, from 2001 to 2018 had "conducted themselves on the clear basis that the fence represented their mutual north-south boundary."

"It was the defendants' unilateral action from May 2018 that disrupted what had been settled for decades," he said. "It follows that Mr and Mrs McCarthy's claims for trespass...are established on the balance of probabilities."

The case is set to return to court in the summer for a hearing to decide the consequences of the ruling against the siblings, including any compensation due and the costs of the case.

News.title: Israel passes law allowing death penalty for Palestinians convicted of murder
News.content:
Israel passes law allowing death penalty for Palestinians convicted of murder

Under the law, West Bank Palestinians convicted of killing Israelis will face hanging - but will only apply to future cases

View 3 Images (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Israel’s parliament has passed a law making the death penalty the default punishment for Palestinians convicted of murdering Israelis.

‌



The bill marks the latest victory for the country’s far-right, which has long pushed for harsher punishments for Palestinians accused of nationalistic attacks. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu attended the vote in person and backed the measure.

‌



Under the law, West Bank Palestinians convicted of killings will face hanging. Israeli courts can also impose the death penalty or life imprisonment on Israeli citizens. The legislation is not retroactive and will apply only to future cases.

‌



Rights groups in Israel and Palestine have condemned the law as racist, draconian, and unlikely to prevent attacks.

View 3 Images (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

When the bill passed, the chamber erupted into cheers. National security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who championed the law, waved a bottle in celebration. Netanyahu remained motionless.

‌



Far-right lawmaker Limor Son Har-Melech, one of the bill’s sponsors, wiped tears from her eyes. Her first husband was killed in a West Bank attack by a Palestinian militant.

Minutes after the vote, the Association of Civil Rights in Israel said it had petitioned the country’s Supreme Court, calling the law “discriminatory by design” and “enacted without legal authority” over West Bank Palestinians.

Executions are set to take place within 30 days of sentencing.

‌



Ben-Gvir, speaking before the vote, described the law as long overdue and a show of national pride. “From today, every terrorist will know, and the whole world will know, that whoever takes a life, the State of Israel will take their life,” he said, wearing his signature lapel pin: a small metal noose.

Critics include Israelis, Palestinians, international rights groups, and the United Nations. They warn the law creates a hierarchy in Israel’s court systems, confining the death penalty largely to Palestinians convicted of murdering Jewish citizens.

Military courts, which try only West Bank Palestinians, will deliver the sentences, though they can commute to life imprisonment in “special circumstances.” Israeli courts, which handle cases involving Israeli citizens, including Palestinian citizens of Israel, can impose life imprisonment or the death penalty in murders intended to harm citizens or challenge Israel’s existence.

‌



View 3 Images (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Experts say the distinction is deeply problematic. Amichai Cohen, senior fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, warned the law applies only in territories with military courts and to attacks motivated by undermining Israel, meaning Jews cannot be sentenced under the law. He added that under international law, Israel should not be legislating in the West Bank.

The parliament’s legal advisers raised concerns that the law denies clemency, contradicting international conventions, and calls for executions within 90 days.

‌



Though Israel technically allows the death penalty for genocide, wartime espionage, and certain terror offences, no one has been executed since Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann in 1962.

The law will not apply to attackers currently held from the October 7, 2023 assault. A separate bill is under consideration for their punishment.

Some opposition lawmakers fear the law could complicate future hostage negotiations. Israel freed thousands of Palestinian prisoners in exchange for roughly 250 hostages taken in the October 2023 attacks.

Article continues below

The Public Committee Against Torture in Israel noted the state has historically voted at the U.N. to abolish the death penalty. Until recently, Shin Bet, Israel’s security agency, also opposed executions, warning they could provoke revenge attacks by Palestinian militants.

News.title: Arsenal football stars address 'shame' in landmark campaign - and it's full of hope
News.content:
Arsenal football stars address 'shame' in landmark campaign - and it's full of hope

Persil's new campaign, The Dirt Is Good, fronted by Beth Mead, has already educated millions of children – and ­families – around one of the last real taboos: menstrual leaks.

View 3 Images Beth Mead stars in Persil's latest campaign, which is built on research showing six in 10 girls are still apprehensive about playing sport because of period stains.

The implications for our kids of last week’s court ruling against Meta and YouTube, for example. Both tech giants were found to be liable for designing their platforms to be addictive. A 20-year-old woman, known as Kaley, is understood to have brought the case that has left Silicon Valley reeling. Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp, and YouTube owner Google have said they will appeal the jury’s verdict, which included £2.3million in compensation and an additional £2.3million in damages.

‌



‌



The terrifying truth is our children’s attention spans are the commodity that the digital big beasts are fighting for. It has been that way for many years. Those carefree dances, pranks and puppies with their cute AI voices might all seem harmless enough. But Kaley’s struggles at school and with her family began after she started using Instagram at the age of nine.

‌



View 3 Images Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg leaves the Federal Courthouse in downtown Los Angeles after defending the company in a landmark social media addiction trial in Los Angeles, United States, on February 19, 2026

So Unilever’s Dirt Is Good campaign, to encourage girls and boys to get outside and embrace grassroots, community and street ­football, is needed more than ever. With a daughter of my own who relishes a run out at the weekend with her team, I’m well aware of the health, social and self-confidence benefits around girls’ football.

There are other benefits too. The Dirt Is Good campaign has already educated millions of children – and ­families – around one of the last real taboos: menstrual leaks. Arsenal players, including Beth Mead and Leah Williamson, backed the campaign to show every stain is part of the game and should not be a source of shame. It is built on research showing six in 10 girls are still apprehensive about playing sport because of period stains.

‌



Unilever, which makes Persil, continues to use real photos of female athletes who have bled during ­competition to make deliberate ­comparisons between the stains we celebrate and the ones society has taught girls to be ashamed of. Arsenal might not be the team I support but I am fully behind the North London club using their Brazilian players, including striker Gabriel Jesus, to help UK kids understand and connect with varzea – the name for Brazilian grassroots football.

View 3 Images Arsenal stars Alessia Russo, Beth Mead and Lotte Wubben-Moy in the landmark Dirt is Good campaign

Women’s football champion Ian Wright travelled out to the Sao Paulo region of the South American country for the Dirt is Good campaign to promote the power of varzea on home soil.

‌



Remarkably, eight grassroots teams in Sao Paulo have Arsenal in their name, having been captivated by the likes of the legendary Invincibles, Jesus, current defender Gabriel Magalhaes and former Brazilian captain Gilberto Silva. (For so many clubs in England, one Arsenal closing in on winning the Premier League title is tough enough!)

So the five-part documentary, Dirt is Glory, following teams from the streets of Brazil competing in the OMO Varzenal Cup for the chance to play at the Emirates Stadium, is also welcome.

In the tug of war for our kids’ attention, the invisible pull of social media remains frighteningly strong. But if children and parents remember the power of sport and getting outside, the best team could win that fight.

News.title: April's full Pink Moon to light up the night sky this week - exact time and date
News.content:
April's full Pink Moon to light up the night sky this week - exact time and date

The Pink Moon will be visible in the UK for three nights from March 31 to April 2, with the best time to see it being in the early hours of Thursday, April 2

View 3 Images April's full Pink Moon is taking place this week (Image: Getty)

A stunning celestial spectacle is set to unfold this week as April's full Pink Moon reaches its peak on Thursday night.

‌



This enchanting lunar phenomenon will appear full for roughly three nights from March 31 through to April 2.

‌



Sky gazers will need to remain awake late or rise in the small hours to witness the Pink Moon at its most brilliant. It will achieve peak illumination on the night of Wednesday, April 1, with its fullest point occurring at 3.12am on Thursday, April 2.

‌



Throughout the evening of April Fool's Day, the moon is expected to appear more orange than pink owing to it ascending low on the horizon.

The Moon may display a different hue because its reflected sunlight travels through a thicker section of Earth's atmosphere, which disperses shorter blue and violet wavelengths, permitting the warmer red tones to reach us.

View 3 Images Its name comes from pink spring wildflowers that bloom during early April (Image: Getty)

‌



Traditionally signalling the onset of Spring in the northern hemisphere, the moon doesn't actually turn pink, despite its name.

Its title derives from pink spring wildflowers that blossom during early April. As it's not a supermoon, it will appear standard in size, reports the Express.

The moon holds numerous spiritual meanings including: renewal and rebirth, releasing the past and growth and clarity. During a full moon, the moon's surface is completely illuminated by the sun.

Article continues below

The pink moon is the fourth of 13 full moons in 2026.

View 3 Images The full Pink Moon will be at its fullest at 3.12am on Thursday April 2 (Image: Getty)

Those hoping to glimpse this beautiful illumination can observe it anywhere in the UK that boasts a clear sky, though open, elevated locations provide a far superior viewing experience. For the optimal view, it's suggested to gaze eastwards at moonrise, select a location devoid of buildings or trees and don't forget to bring along a pair of binoculars.

News.title: James Stannage dead: Legendary radio host dies as tributes pour in for 'unmissable' DJ
News.content:
A legendary Manchester radio host has died. James Stannage, who fans said was 'unmissable' and had a 'brutal' and 'savage' approach to hosting his show, was 76 when he died.

Stannage was known for hosting a late-night phone-in show in the mid 1970s that had a 'no nonsense' attitude to calls. He went on to appear on Picadilly Radio and Key 103 from the 1970s to the 2000s. He left Key 103 in 2005 after his "savage" style caused the radio station to be fined £125,000.

The radio station received several fines during his 20-year career on the station. In November 2005, he read out the comments and jokes submitted by a listener about the death of Ken Bigley, leading to the final fine.

Ensure our latest headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as your Preferred Source in your Google search settings.

Image: facebook) facebook)





Despite his controversial time on Key 103, fans remembered him warmly in tributes posted to Facebook. One wrote: "RIP local radio legend James Stannage. Many of us out there hold great memories of listening to him growing up in the Manchester area."

Another added: "Back in the days when Piccadilly radio was unrivalled, his late show was unmissable." A third said they had "so much fun listening" to him as a child and that "he was brutal". A fourth said that "he could be savage".

One fan also said Stannage was a "true king" of radio: "Sad news that Manchester radio legend James Stannage has passed away. The true king of late night on Piccadilly when I worked in the area."

Stannage's son Darren confirmed his death on Monday morning. Stannage died following a year-long battle with cancer and Darren described him as "someone who meant so much to so many people in Manchester".

Image: Wikipedia) Wikipedia)

Darren said on Facebook: "It is with great sadness that today cancer took another victim. This time it was a partner, a dad, a grandad and a brother. Also someone who meant to so much to so many people in Manchester as my Dad James Stannage has passed away.

"He died peacefully this morning at MRI after battling cancer for over a year. Listening to The Who, he was surrounded by people that loved him and died at 1152am. Such a remarkable time as that was the Radio Station that made him a legend in Manchester to so many people who grew up listening to him on Piccadilly and later on Key 103.

"There will be so many stories and memories that people will have. I will miss him so much as I know so many people will and am very lucky to ahve been able to have called him my Dad. X"
